name: Eagle Lunar Module descent stage
statusNote: The descent stage has stood at Tranquility Base since 1969. The laser retroreflector the crew set up nearby is still used by scientists today.

location.description: Tranquility Base, Sea of Tranquility (Mare Tranquillitatis)

tagline: The landing legs that carried the first people to walk on the Moon.
story: Meet Eagle's descent stage: the bottom half of the lunar module that landed Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon on 20 July 1969.
The descent stage had a rocket engine that slowed Eagle down as it dropped towards the Moon. Armstrong steered past a field of boulders and touched down with only a little fuel left.

When it was time to go home, the top half (the ascent stage) blasted off and used the descent stage as its launch pad. The descent stage stayed behind, and it is still there today with a plaque on one of its legs.
objectives: Land two astronauts safely on the Moon and return them to Earth
Collect samples of Moon rock and soil
Set up the first science experiments on the lunar surface

instruments.name: Laser Ranging Retroreflector
instruments.purpose: A panel of special mirrors that bounces laser light from Earth straight back, so scientists can measure the distance to the Moon very precisely.

instruments.name: Passive Seismic Experiment
instruments.purpose: A seismometer that listened for moonquakes and meteorite impacts for a few weeks.

instruments.name: Solar Wind Composition experiment
instruments.purpose: A sheet of aluminium foil that caught tiny particles streaming from the Sun. The astronauts brought it back to Earth for study.

discoveries: Humans walked on another world for the first time.
The crew brought back about 21.5 kg of Moon rocks and soil, including volcanic rocks formed from ancient lava.
Laser measurements using the retroreflector show the Moon is slowly moving away from Earth, by about 3.8 cm each year.

Spacecraft enters orbit around the Moon
Eagle lands in the Sea of Tranquility
Armstrong and Aldrin explore the surface and set up experiments
Ascent stage lifts off; the descent stage stays behind
The crew splashes down safely on Earth

funFact: A plaque on Eagle's leg says the astronauts 'came in peace for all mankind'.

name: Intrepid Lunar Module descent stage
statusNote: The descent stage has stood in the Ocean of Storms since 1969, about 180 m from the Surveyor 3 robot lander. The science station the crew set up sent data until 30 September 1977.

location.description: Ocean of Storms (Oceanus Procellarum), about 180 m from Surveyor 3

tagline: The pinpoint landing next to an old robot friend.
story: Meet Intrepid's descent stage: the bottom half of the lunar module that landed Pete Conrad and Alan Bean on the Moon on 19 November 1969, while Richard Gordon circled overhead in the command module.

Apollo 11 had landed a long way from its target. Apollo 12 had to prove astronauts could land exactly where they aimed, and Intrepid came down within about 180 m of Surveyor 3, a robot lander that had arrived two and a half years earlier.
The crew spent 31 hours and 31 minutes on the Moon. When they left, the top half (the ascent stage) carried them back up, and the descent stage stayed behind for good.
objectives: Make a pinpoint landing close to the Surveyor 3 robot lander
Set up a long-lasting science station on the Moon
Bring home parts of Surveyor 3 to see how materials change on the Moon

instruments.name: Passive seismometer
instruments.purpose: Felt moonquakes and impacts. It was part of a science station that sent data to Earth until 1977.

instruments.name: Lunar surface magnetometer
instruments.purpose: Measured the Moon's magnetic field at the landing site.

instruments.name: Solar wind spectrometer
instruments.purpose: Measured the stream of particles flowing out from the Sun.

discoveries: Astronauts could land exactly where they planned: Intrepid touched down within about 180 m of Surveyor 3.
The crew brought back 34.35 kg of Moon rocks and soil, plus Surveyor 3's camera and soil scoop.
When the empty ascent stage was crashed into the Moon on purpose, the seismometer kept recording signals for nearly an hour.

Intrepid lands in the Ocean of Storms, close to Surveyor 3
First moonwalk: the crew sets up the science station
Second moonwalk: the crew visits Surveyor 3 and removes its camera and scoop
Ascent stage lifts off; it is later crashed on purpose as a test moonquake
The science station is switched off

funFact: Intrepid's empty top half was crashed into the Moon on purpose, so the seismometer could feel a moonquake of known size and timing.

name: Antares Lunar Module descent stage
statusNote: The descent stage has stood in the hilly Fra Mauro region since 1971. The top half was crashed into the Moon on purpose after the crew left.

location.description: Fra Mauro highlands, about 24 km north of Fra Mauro crater

tagline: The lander that helped make a moonquake on purpose.
story: Meet Antares's descent stage: the bottom half of the lunar module that landed Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell on the Moon on 5 February 1971. Stuart Roosa stayed in orbit in the command module Kitty Hawk.

Antares landed in the hilly upland region north of Fra Mauro crater. The crew stayed a record 33 hours and 30 minutes and made two moonwalks, setting up a science station and pulling their tools along in an equipment cart.

After the crew flew back up, the empty top half (the ascent stage) was steered to crash into the Moon on purpose. Seismometers at the Apollo 12 and Apollo 14 sites felt the shaking for 1.5 hours. The descent stage is still at Fra Mauro.
objectives: Explore the hilly Fra Mauro region
Set up a science station on the Moon
Collect rocks and soil and take photographs, on the surface and from orbit

instruments.name: Passive seismometer
instruments.purpose: Felt moonquakes and impacts, including the crash of Antares's own top half.

instruments.name: Laser ranging retroreflector
instruments.purpose: Special mirrors that bounce laser light from Earth straight back, to measure the distance to the Moon.

instruments.name: Lunar portable magnetometer
instruments.purpose: A carry-along instrument that measured magnetism at different places.

instruments.name: Modular Equipment Transporter
instruments.purpose: An equipment cart the astronauts used to carry tools and samples.

discoveries: The crew collected 42.28 kg of Moon rocks and soil and walked about 3.45 km during their moonwalks.
The planned crash of the ascent stage gave scientists a moonquake of known size, which two seismometers recorded for 1.5 hours.
Seeds carried around the Moon by Stuart Roosa were later grown into 'Moon Trees' and planted across the United States.

funFact: Command module pilot Stuart Roosa carried about 500 tree seeds around the Moon. Trees grown from them are called Moon Trees.

name: Falcon Lunar Module descent stage
statusNote: The descent stage has stood at Hadley–Apennine since 1971, with the parked Lunar Roving Vehicle nearby. The science station the crew set up sent data until 30 September 1977.

location.description: Hadley–Apennine, at the foot of the Apennine Mountains near Hadley Rille

tagline: The lander that brought the first car to the Moon.
story: Meet Falcon's descent stage: the bottom half of the lunar module that landed David Scott and James Irwin on the Moon on 30 July 1971, while Alfred Worden orbited above in the command module.

Falcon carried something new folded up on its side: the Lunar Roving Vehicle. With the rover, the crew could explore much farther, driving about 27.9 km in three trips near Hadley Rille and the Apennine Mountains.
The crew stayed 66 hours and 55 minutes. Then the top half (the ascent stage) carried them back to orbit, and the descent stage stayed behind for good.
objectives: Explore Hadley Rille and the Apennine Mountains using the first Moon car
Set up a seven-instrument science station
Collect rocks from many different places

instruments.name: Passive seismometer
instruments.purpose: Felt moonquakes and impacts until the station was switched off in 1977.

instruments.name: Heat flow experiment
instruments.purpose: Measured how much heat flows out from inside the Moon.

instruments.name: Lunar surface magnetometer
instruments.purpose: Measured the Moon's magnetic field at the landing site.

instruments.name: Lunar Roving Vehicle
instruments.purpose: A folding electric car that carried the astronauts and their tools across the Moon.

discoveries: With the rover, the crew drove about 27.9 km in three trips and stayed within 5 km of Falcon.
They brought back 77.31 kg of Moon rocks and soil.
The empty ascent stage crashed into the Moon on 3 August 1971 at 26.36° N, 0.25° E, giving the seismometers another known impact to study.

name: Lunar Roving Vehicle 1
statusNote: Parked near the lunar module's landing site since 1971. It no longer works, but it is still there.

location.description: Hadley–Apennine region, near Hadley Rille

tagline: The first car ever driven on the Moon.
story: Meet the first Moon buggy! Apollo 15 brought a folded-up, battery-powered car to the Moon. Astronauts David Scott and James Irwin unfolded it and drove off to explore.
With the rover, the astronauts could travel much farther than on foot. They drove to the edge of a giant valley called Hadley Rille and up the slopes of the Apennine Mountains.
At the end, they parked the rover where its TV camera could film their lift-off. Then it stayed behind for good.
objectives: Carry astronauts and tools much farther across the Moon than they could walk
Explore Hadley Rille and the Apennine Mountains
Collect rocks from many different places

instruments.name: Colour TV camera
instruments.purpose: Controlled from Earth, it sent live pictures of the astronauts at work and filmed the lift-off.

instruments.name: Navigation system
instruments.purpose: Tracked direction and distance so the astronauts could always find their way back to the lunar module.

discoveries: The astronauts drove about 27.9 km across the Moon over three trips.
They found the 'Genesis Rock', a piece of the Moon's very ancient crust.
The mission showed that a rover could greatly expand how much of the Moon astronauts could explore.

timeline.label: Apollo 15 launches
Lunar module Falcon lands at Hadley–Apennine
First drive of a car on the Moon
Genesis Rock collected during the second drive
Rover's camera films the lift-off; the rover stays behind

funFact: The rover folded up like a deck chair so it could fit in a compartment on the side of the lunar module.

name: Surveyor 3
statusNote: Silent since May 1967. Astronauts visited it in 1969 and brought some of its parts back to Earth.

location.description: Ocean of Storms (Oceanus Procellarum)

tagline: The robot that got a visit from astronauts.
story: Before people could land on the Moon, NASA had to answer a big question: is the ground solid enough to stand on? Surveyor 3 was sent to find out.
It had a little scoop on a mechanical arm. Engineers on Earth used it to dig trenches and poke the soil, and its camera sent back thousands of pictures.

Two and a half years later, Apollo 12 landed close by. Astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean walked over to Surveyor 3 and cut off its camera and other parts to bring home, so scientists could see how materials change on the Moon.
objectives: Prove a spacecraft could land softly on the Moon
Test whether lunar soil could hold up a crewed spacecraft
Take pictures of the landing area

instruments.name: TV camera
instruments.purpose: Took thousands of pictures of the surface around the lander.

instruments.name: Surface sampler
instruments.purpose: A scoop on an arm that dug trenches to test how firm the soil was.

discoveries: The Moon's soil behaved like wet sand and was firm enough to hold up an Apollo lunar module.
It was the first spacecraft to dig into the surface of another world: it dug four trenches with its scoop.
Its camera took 6,326 pictures, and parts returned by Apollo 12 helped scientists study how materials age on the Moon.

timeline.label: Surveyor 3 launches
Lands in the Ocean of Storms, bouncing before it settles
Digs trenches and takes thousands of pictures
Last contact with Earth
Apollo 12 astronauts visit and remove parts to bring home

funFact: Its engine did not shut off at the right moment, so Surveyor 3 bounced twice, about 10 m and then about 3 m high, before it settled.

name: Lunokhod 1
statusNote: Stopped working in 1971. Its laser reflector was found again in NASA spacecraft images in 2010 and has been used for laser ranging since.

location.description: Sea of Rains (Mare Imbrium)

tagline: The first robot rover to drive on another world.
story: This one is not from NASA, but it is too important to leave out. Lunokhod 1 was built by the Soviet Union, and it was the first remote-controlled robot to drive on another world.
It looked like a bathtub on eight wheels. A team on Earth steered it using pictures from its cameras, even though every picture took time to arrive.
Lunokhod 1 explored for about ten months. Years later, NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed it from above, and scientists started bouncing lasers off its mirror again.
objectives: Drive a robot on the Moon, controlled from Earth
Photograph the surface and study the soil
Carry a laser reflector for measuring the Earth–Moon distance

instruments.name: TV cameras
instruments.purpose: Helped the drivers on Earth see where to steer, and photographed the landscape.

instruments.name: X-ray fluorescence spectrometer
instruments.purpose: Measured which chemical elements are in the lunar soil.

instruments.name: Penetrometer
instruments.purpose: Pushed into the ground to test how firm it was.

instruments.name: Laser retroreflector
instruments.purpose: French-built mirrors for measuring the distance to the Moon.

discoveries: Showed that a robot could be driven on another world from Earth.
Travelled about 10.5 km and studied the soil at many stops.

timeline.label: Luna 17 launches from the Soviet Union
Lands in the Sea of Rains; Lunokhod 1 rolls off
Last contact with Earth
Located in images from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter

funFact: Lunokhod 1 had a lid covered in solar cells that opened during the lunar day and closed at night to keep it warm.

name: LCROSS
missionName: Lunar Crater Observation and Sensing Satellite
statusNote: Crashed into the Moon on purpose in 2009, as planned, after studying the cloud made by its rocket stage.

location.description: Cabeus crater, near the Moon's south pole

tagline: The spacecraft that crashed on purpose to find water.
story: Some craters near the Moon's poles are so deep that sunlight never reaches their floors. Scientists wondered: could ice be hiding there?

LCROSS had a clever plan. First, its empty rocket stage smashed into Cabeus crater, throwing up a giant cloud. Then LCROSS flew straight through the cloud, measuring what was inside, before crashing in too.
Its instruments found water in that cloud. Water on the Moon could one day help astronauts make drinking water, air and even rocket fuel.
objectives: Find out if water ice is hidden in permanently shadowed craters
Study the cloud thrown up by a deliberate impact

instruments.name: Cameras (visible and infrared)
instruments.purpose: Watched the impact and the cloud of material it threw up.

instruments.name: Spectrometers
instruments.purpose: Split light into colours to find out what the cloud was made of, including water.

discoveries: Found water in the material thrown up from Cabeus crater.
Showed that shadowed polar craters can trap water and other substances for a very long time.

timeline.label: Launches together with the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
Rocket stage hits Cabeus crater; LCROSS flies through the cloud
LCROSS itself impacts minutes later, as planned

funFact: LCROSS had about four minutes to study the cloud before it crashed into the Moon itself.

name: Viking 1 lander
statusNote: Contact was lost in November 1982 after a faulty command was sent from Earth.

location.description: Chryse Planitia (Plains of Gold)

tagline: The first U.S. spacecraft to land safely on Mars.
story: In 1976, Viking 1 became the first American spacecraft to land safely on Mars. Within minutes it sent home the first picture ever taken from the Martian surface.
Viking 1 had a mini laboratory on board. It scooped up soil and ran experiments to look for signs of tiny living things.
The results were puzzling and did not give clear proof of life. But Viking 1 kept working and reporting Martian weather for more than six years.
objectives: Land safely and photograph the surface of Mars
Search the soil for signs of life
Study Martian weather and the ground

instruments.name: Cameras
instruments.purpose: Took the first pictures from the surface of Mars.

instruments.name: Biology experiments
instruments.purpose: Mixed soil with nutrients and gases to look for signs of living things.

instruments.name: Gas chromatograph–mass spectrometer
instruments.purpose: Searched the soil for carbon-based chemicals.

instruments.name: Weather station
instruments.purpose: Measured temperature, pressure and wind every day.

discoveries: Sent the first images from the surface of Mars.
Its soil tests did not find clear evidence of life, which shaped how later missions searched.
Recorded years of Martian weather.

timeline.label: Viking 1 launches
Enters orbit around Mars
Lander touches down in Chryse Planitia

funFact: The Viking 1 lander was powered by small nuclear generators instead of solar panels.

name: Mars Pathfinder lander
statusNote: Last heard from on 27 September 1997, after working three times longer than planned.

location.description: Ares Vallis

tagline: The lander that bounced onto Mars inside giant airbags.
story: On 4 July 1997, Mars Pathfinder did something nobody had tried before: it landed on Mars wrapped in giant airbags, bouncing across the ground like a beach ball before rolling to a stop.
Then its petals opened like a flower and a tiny rover named Sojourner drove down a ramp. The lander became the rover's base station, sending its messages to Earth.
Pathfinder photographed its landing site, which showed signs that a huge flood once rushed through the area long ago.
objectives: Test a new low-cost way of landing on Mars using airbags
Deliver and support the Sojourner rover
Study Mars's rocks, soil and weather

instruments.name: Imager for Mars Pathfinder
instruments.purpose: A stereo camera on a mast that photographed the landing site in 3D.

instruments.name: Atmospheric and weather package
instruments.purpose: Measured temperature, pressure and wind.

discoveries: Proved the airbag landing system, later used by the Spirit and Opportunity rovers.
Rounded pebbles and the shapes of the land suggested that water once flowed there in a giant flood.

timeline.label: Mars Pathfinder launches
Bounces to a landing in Ares Vallis
Sojourner rolls onto the Martian surface
Last contact with Earth

funFact: After landing, the lander was renamed the Carl Sagan Memorial Station after the famous astronomer.

name: Sojourner rover
statusNote: Sojourner talked to Earth through the Pathfinder lander. When the lander went silent in 1997, contact with Sojourner was lost too.

location.description: Near the Pathfinder lander in Ares Vallis

tagline: The first rover on Mars, about the size of a microwave oven.
story: Meet Sojourner, one of humanity's first robotic explorers on Mars. It was small, light, and had six wheels.

NASA sent Sojourner to prove that a rover could drive on Mars and study rocks up close. Drivers on Earth chose where it should go, and Sojourner used its own sensors to avoid bumping into rocks on the way.
Sojourner pressed its science instrument against rocks the team nicknamed 'Barnacle Bill' and 'Yogi' to find out what they were made of. Every rover on Mars since has followed in its tracks.
objectives: Prove that a small rover could move around and work on Mars
Measure what Martian rocks and soil are made of
Test how wheels behave on Martian ground

instruments.name: Alpha Proton X-ray Spectrometer (APXS)
instruments.purpose: Measured the chemical elements in rocks and soil.

instruments.name: Cameras
instruments.purpose: Helped with driving and photographed rocks up close.

discoveries: Became the first wheeled vehicle to explore another planet.
Found that some rocks were richer in silica than scientists expected, hinting that Mars's history was more complicated than thought.
Showed that a rover could partly drive itself, which helped every later Mars rover.

timeline.label: Launches aboard Mars Pathfinder
Arrives on Mars, folded up on the lander
Drives down the ramp onto Mars
Studies the rocks 'Barnacle Bill' and 'Yogi'
Contact lost when the lander goes silent

funFact: Sojourner was named after Sojourner Truth, an American who fought for freedom and equal rights.

name: Spirit rover
statusNote: Got stuck in soft sand in 2009 and last contacted Earth on 22 March 2010. NASA ended the mission in May 2011.

location.description: Landed in Gusev crater. Final resting place: a site called Troy, near the Columbia Hills.

tagline: The rover that dug up clues of ancient hot springs.
story: Spirit was planned to work for just 90 Martian days. It kept going for more than six years!
Spirit explored a giant crater called Gusev. When one of its six wheels stopped turning, the team drove it backwards, dragging the broken wheel.
That dragging wheel scraped up bright white soil that turned out to be almost pure silica. On Earth, that kind of soil forms near hot springs or steam vents, places where tiny life can thrive.
objectives: Search rocks and soil for evidence of past water
Explore Gusev crater and the Columbia Hills
Test how long a solar-powered rover could survive on Mars

instruments.name: Panoramic camera (Pancam)
instruments.purpose: Took colour panoramas of the landscape.

instruments.name: Rock Abrasion Tool
instruments.purpose: Ground away the dusty outside of rocks to see the fresh rock inside.

instruments.name: Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer
instruments.purpose: Measured the chemical elements in rocks and soil.

instruments.name: Mössbauer spectrometer
instruments.purpose: Identified iron-bearing minerals.

instruments.name: Microscopic Imager
instruments.purpose: Took close-up pictures of rock grains, like a geologist's hand lens.

discoveries: Found nearly pure silica deposits, a sign of ancient hot springs or steam vents.
Found rocks changed by water in the Columbia Hills.
Drove about 7.7 km in total.

Bounces to a landing in Gusev crater

Broken wheel uncovers nearly pure silica soil

funFact: Gusts of Martian wind sometimes blew dust off Spirit's solar panels, giving it a surprise power boost.

name: Opportunity rover
statusNote: A planet-wide dust storm blocked sunlight from its solar panels. Its last contact was on 10 June 2018, and NASA ended the mission in February 2019.

location.description: Landed in Eagle crater, Meridiani Planum. Final resting place: Perseverance Valley on the rim of Endeavour crater.

tagline: Built to last 90 Martian days, it kept exploring for more than 14 years.
story: Opportunity was the twin of Spirit. It landed on the other side of Mars and rolled into a small crater, right next to a layer of bedrock. Scientists called it a 'hole in one'!
Close up, the rocks were full of tiny grey balls nicknamed 'blueberries'. They are made of a mineral called hematite, which usually forms in water.
Opportunity kept driving for more than 14 years and covered over 45 km. In 2018, a huge dust storm darkened the sky, and its solar-powered batteries could not recharge.
objectives: Search for evidence that water once existed on Mars
Study rocks and soil in Meridiani Planum
Explore as long and as far as possible

instruments.name: Panoramic camera (Pancam)
instruments.purpose: Took colour panoramas of the landscape.

instruments.name: Rock Abrasion Tool
instruments.purpose: Ground away the outside of rocks to see the fresh rock inside.

instruments.name: Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer
instruments.purpose: Measured the chemical elements in rocks.

instruments.name: Mössbauer spectrometer
instruments.purpose: Identified iron minerals, including hematite.

instruments.name: Microscopic Imager
instruments.purpose: Took close-up pictures of rock grains.

discoveries: Hematite 'blueberries' and layered rocks showed that liquid water once soaked the ground.
Found veins of gypsum, a mineral left behind by water flowing through cracks.
Drove about 45 km, farther than any rover before it.

Lands in Eagle crater, Meridiani Planum

name: Phoenix lander
statusNote: Stopped talking to Earth in November 2008 as the arctic winter set in. Later pictures showed ice had damaged its solar panels.

location.description: Vastitas Borealis, Mars's northern arctic plains

tagline: The lander that touched ice on Mars.
story: Phoenix landed farther north than any Mars spacecraft before, in a flat arctic plain covered with polygon-shaped cracks.

With its robotic arm, Phoenix dug into the ground and uncovered bright white patches. Days later some of the patches had disappeared. They were water ice, turning straight into vapour in the sunlight!
Phoenix also watched snow falling from Martian clouds. As winter came, the Sun stopped rising, and Phoenix went quiet.
objectives: Dig up and study ice under the surface
Find out whether the soil could ever have supported tiny life
Study the weather in Mars's arctic

instruments.name: Robotic arm
instruments.purpose: Dug trenches and delivered samples to the instruments on deck.

instruments.name: Thermal and Evolved Gas Analyzer (TEGA)
instruments.purpose: Baked soil samples in tiny ovens to see what gases came out.

instruments.name: Wet chemistry lab (MECA)
instruments.purpose: Mixed soil with water to measure its chemistry.

instruments.name: Weather station with lidar
instruments.purpose: Used a laser to study clouds and dust in the sky.

discoveries: Confirmed water ice just below the surface of Mars's arctic.
Found perchlorate, a salt that affects how scientists search for life.
Saw snow falling from clouds, although it vanished before reaching the ground.

timeline.label: Phoenix launches
Lands using rocket engines in the northern plains
Ice seen vanishing from a trench confirms water ice
Last signal as winter begins
NASA ends the mission after failed attempts to make contact

funFact: Phoenix carried a mini DVD with stories and messages about Mars, as a gift for future explorers.

name: InSight lander
missionName: Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy and Heat Transport
statusNote: Dust slowly covered its solar panels. After it missed two contact attempts, NASA ended the mission on 21 December 2022.

location.description: Elysium Planitia

tagline: The lander that listened to marsquakes.
story: Every other Mars mission looked at the surface. InSight wanted to know what Mars is like deep inside.

It placed a super-sensitive seismometer on the ground and covered it with a dome to block the wind. Then it listened. When Mars shook, waves travelled through the planet, and their echoes revealed what lies underneath.
InSight heard more than 1,300 marsquakes. Using them, scientists measured the size of Mars's core for the first time.
objectives: Study the deep interior of Mars: crust, mantle and core
Measure marsquakes and meteorite impacts
Measure how heat flows out of the planet

instruments.name: SEIS seismometer
instruments.purpose: Listened for marsquakes and impacts. It was sensitive enough to feel vibrations smaller than an atom.

instruments.name: HP3 heat probe ('the mole')
instruments.purpose: Tried to hammer itself deep underground to measure heat. The soil turned out to be too clumpy for it to dig deep.

instruments.name: RISE radio experiment
instruments.purpose: Tracked tiny wobbles in Mars's spin to learn about its core.

instruments.name: Weather sensors
instruments.purpose: Measured wind, temperature and air pressure.

discoveries: Detected more than 1,300 marsquakes.
Found that Mars has a liquid metal core and measured how big it is.
Mapped the layers of Mars's crust.

timeline.label: InSight launches
Lands in Elysium Planitia
Records its first likely marsquake
Records the largest marsquake ever detected
Last contact with Earth
NASA ends the mission

funFact: InSight's seismometer was so sensitive that it could also feel the wind and passing dust devils.

name: Voyager 1
statusNote: Still sending data from interstellar space. To save power, engineers have switched off most instruments; in April 2026 they turned off another, leaving two science instruments running.

location.description: Interstellar space, beyond the heliopause

trajectory: Travelling out of the solar system. In late 2026 its radio signals take about a whole day to reach Earth.
tagline: The farthest human-made object, still talking to Earth.
story: Voyager 1 launched in 1977, before most of your parents were born! It flew past Jupiter and Saturn and sent home amazing close-up pictures.
Then it kept going. In 2012 it became the first spacecraft to reach interstellar space, the region between the stars, beyond the bubble the Sun blows around our solar system.

Voyager 1 carries a golden record with sounds and pictures of Earth, in case anyone ever finds it. Its power drops a little every year, so engineers switch off instruments one by one to keep it talking as long as possible.
objectives: Fly past and study Jupiter and Saturn and their moons
Study the outer edge of the Sun's influence

name: Voyager 2
statusNote: Still sending data from interstellar space. Several instruments have been switched off to save power.

location.description: Interstellar space, beyond the heliopause

trajectory: Travelling out of the solar system, below the plane in which the planets orbit.
tagline: The only spacecraft ever to visit Uranus and Neptune.
story: Voyager 2 actually launched 16 days before its twin, Voyager 1. It took a longer path that let it visit all four giant planets.
Using the gravity of each planet like a slingshot, it flew past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. No other spacecraft has ever been to Uranus or Neptune.
In 2018 it followed Voyager 1 into interstellar space. It also carries a golden record full of greetings, music and sounds from Earth.
objectives: Visit Jupiter and Saturn, then Uranus and Neptune
Study the giant planets' moons, rings and magnetic fields
Explore the edge of the Sun's influence and beyond

name: Pioneer 10
statusNote: Its last, very weak signal was received on 23 January 2003. Its power source had grown too weak to answer again.

location.description: Far beyond the planets, heading out of the solar system

trajectory: Coasting in the direction of the red star Aldebaran, in the constellation Taurus.
tagline: The first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and visit Jupiter.
story: In 1972, nobody knew if a spacecraft could survive a trip through the asteroid belt. Pioneer 10 went first, and made it through safely.
In 1973 it became the first spacecraft to fly past Jupiter, taking close-up pictures and measuring the planet's powerful radiation.
Pioneer 10 carries a metal plaque with a drawing of a man and a woman and a map showing where Earth is, like a message in a bottle.
objectives: Find out if spacecraft could safely cross the asteroid belt
Make the first close-up study of Jupiter
Study the solar wind far from the Sun

name: Pioneer 11
statusNote: Contact ended on 30 September 1995, when its power was too low to keep working.

location.description: Far beyond the planets, heading out of the solar system

trajectory: Coasting in the direction of the constellation Aquila (the Eagle).
tagline: The first spacecraft to visit Saturn.
story: Pioneer 11 followed its twin, Pioneer 10, past Jupiter. It flew even closer, then used Jupiter's gravity to swing all the way across the solar system to Saturn.
In 1979 it became the first spacecraft to visit Saturn. It discovered a new ring and showed the way for the Voyager probes coming after it.
Like Pioneer 10, it carries a plaque with a message from Earth.
objectives: Study Jupiter up close

name: Cassini
agency: NASA, ESA and the Italian Space Agency
statusNote: Ended on purpose on 15 September 2017 by diving into Saturn, so it could never crash into and contaminate moons that might be habitable.

location.description: Burned up in Saturn's atmosphere

tagline: The orbiter that found an ocean hiding inside a moon.
story: Cassini travelled almost seven years to reach Saturn. It carried a passenger: the European Huygens probe, which parachuted down onto Saturn's giant moon Titan.
For 13 years Cassini looped around Saturn. It flew through jets of icy spray shooting out of a small moon called Enceladus, and found they come from a salty ocean beneath the ice.
When its fuel was nearly gone, the team steered Cassini into Saturn on purpose. That way it could never crash into Enceladus or Titan, places that might be able to support life.
objectives: Study Saturn, its rings and its moons up close
Deliver the Huygens probe to Titan
Investigate whether Saturn's moons could support life

discoveries: Found jets of water spraying from Enceladus, fed by an ocean under its ice.

Discovered new moons and learned how Saturn's rings change.

name: New Horizons
statusNote: Still working and exploring the Kuiper Belt, the icy region beyond Neptune.

location.description: The Kuiper Belt, beyond Neptune

trajectory: Travelling outward through the Kuiper Belt.
tagline: The first spacecraft to visit Pluto.
story: When New Horizons launched in 2006, Pluto was just a blurry dot in even the best telescopes. Nobody knew what it really looked like.
After a journey of nine and a half years, New Horizons zoomed past Pluto in July 2015. Pluto had a giant heart-shaped plain of frozen nitrogen and mountains made of water ice!
Then it kept going, and in 2019 it flew past Arrokoth, the most distant object any spacecraft has ever visited up close.
objectives: Make the first close-up study of Pluto and its moons
Explore objects in the Kuiper Belt
